power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is characterized by abnormal dilation and functional remodelling of the thoracic aorta.
Current detection and surveillance rely largely on imaging, limiting population-wide risk stratification.
Circulating proteins may provide biological insight into aortic remodelling and support future biomarker development.
We aimed to identify circulating proteomic patterns associated with imaging-derived thoracic aortic diameter and aortic stiffness in a large population-based cohort.
Methods: A proteome-wide association study was conducted in 6773 UK Biobank participants with available plasma proteomic and cardiac imaging data.

A combined thoracic aortic diameter was derived from taking the maximum of standardized ascending and descending measurements, while stiffness was derived using a pressure-free index of aortic wall properties.
Associations with 2920 circulating proteins were evaluated using multivariable linear regression with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction.
Functional enrichment analysis was performed using the complete ranked protein list across Hallmark, curated, and Gene Ontology Biological Process collections.
Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed as a secondary analysis to explore shared and divergent variation between the two phenotypes.
Results: In age-and sex-adjusted analyses, 358 proteins were associated with aortic diameter and 60 with stiffness after FDR correction.
Sequential adjustment materially altered these associations; in the primary fully adjusted models, 417 proteins were associated with diameter and six with stiffness.
Functional enrichment analyses highlighted complement/coagulation, extracellular matrix organization, and contractile pathways associated with aortic diameter.

In contrast, although only a few individual proteins were associated with stiffness, rank-based pathway analysis across the full proteome identified a distinct enrichment pattern involving cytokine signalling, protein processing, and intracellular transport.
Aortic diameter and stiffness were only modestly correlated (r = 0.21).
Secondary PCA showed that the first principal component (PC1) largely overlapped with the diameter-associated profile, with 310 of 370 PC1-associated proteins also associated with diameter.
Four proteins (REN, BCAN, GGH and THY1) were associated with both diameter and stiffness in addition to being associated with PC1.
Conclusion: Circulating proteomic profiling identified markedly different and minimally overlapping molecular patterns associated with thoracic aortic diameter and stiffness.

Structural dilation was primarily linked to complement/coagulation, extracellular matrix, and contractile pathways, whereas stiffness reflected a smaller, more distinct aspect of aortic remodelling involving cytokine signalling and cellular transport processes.
The four shared proteins across both phenotypes (REN, BCAN, GGH and THY1) represent candidates for further biomarker and causal investigation.

Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is a life-threatening vascular condition characterized by the abnormal focal dilation of the thoracic aorta, encompassing the aortic root, ascending aorta, aortic arch, and descending aorta.
TAAs rarely manifest with symptoms but can continue to enlarge until they rupture, at which point the mortality can exceed 90-97% without immediate intervention due to fatal haemorrhage (1).

text.text: It also remains unclear whether the correlates of thoracic aortic dilation overlap with, or differ from, those from thoracic aortic stiffness.

Therefore, this study was designed to analyse the extensive proteomics data and imaging-derived aortic phenotypes held in the UK Biobank to identify biologically relevant associations between circulating proteins and thoracic aortic diameter and/or stiffness.

By also taking into consideration the overlap between proteins associated with structural dilation and functional stiffening, we aimed to distinguish between shared and phenotype-specific proteomic signatures of thoracic aortic remodelling.
The UK Biobank is a population-based cohort of over 500,000 volunteers, aged 40-69 at baseline (predominantly of self-reported white ethnicity), who were recruited between 2006 and 2010 (17).

The UK Biobank was approved by the North West Research Ethics Committee (21/NW/0157), and all participants provided informed consent at recruitment.
Baseline characteristics were collected during the first assessment visit.
The covariates used in the analysis include age, sex, body mass index (BMI), systolic blood pressure (SBP), smoking status, and ethnicity.

text.text: Hence, a unit increase in the Z-score corresponds to a 1standard-deviation increase in the aortic phenotype.

A combined thoracic aortic diameter phenotype was defined as the maximum of the ascending and descending diameter Z-scores to capture the peak regional abnormality from the imaging reference population.

Aortic stiffness was quantified using a pressure-independent index, which was calculated from ascending aortic diameter obtained from aortic CMR imaging together with the systolic and diastolic blood pressure measurements (25).

text.text: Distributions of the diameter and stiffness phenotypes were assessed using histograms and quantilequantile plots to verify that they followed an approximately Gaussian distribution prior to regression analysis.
The primary analysis of the thoracic aortic phenotype was evaluated across two levels: thoracic aortic diameter and aortic stiffness.
Their association with circulating protein levels was assessed using multivariable linear regression models implemented through the "data.table" R package (26).

text.text: Protein measurements were standardized within each protein target group to account for cross-protein effect comparisons.

To assess proteomic associations with the respective aortic phenotype, sequential covariate-adjustment models were fitted to assess the extent to which BMI and SBP influenced protein-aortic phenotype associations.
The adjustments for age and sex were considered the baseline adjustment set given the well-established associations with both circulating protein levels (27, 28).
text.formatted: The adjustments for age and sex were considered the baseline adjustment set given the well-established associations with both circulating protein levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">28)</ref>.

text.text: For each phenotype, Model 1 was adjusted for age and sex; Model 2 was adjusted for age, sex and BMI; Model 3 was adjusted for age, sex, and SBP; Model 4 included age, sex, BMI and SBP; and Model 5 included further adjustments for smoking status and ethnicity.
This sequential approach was used to evaluate changes in the magnitude of protein-phenotype associations following adjustment for BMI and SBP individually and in combination.
For aortic stiffness, SBP-adjusted models were interpreted as sensitivity analyses given that blood pressure is directly involved in the calculation of the stiffness phenotype.
Therefore, an additional fully adjusted stiffness model (Model 6) was fitted to include age, sex, BMI, smoking status and ethnicity to prevent potential overadjustment.
The false discovery rate (FDR) was accounted for by adjusting raw p-values across all models according to the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method (29).
text.formatted: The false discovery rate (FDR) was accounted for by adjusting raw p-values across all models according to the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) method <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(29)</ref>.

text.text: Results were considered statistically significant at an FDR-adjusted p-value < 0.05.
text.formatted: Results were considered statistically significant at an FDR-adjusted p-value < 0.05.

text.text: As an exploratory analysis, a principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on a unified covariance matrix including both normalized stiffness and combined diameter measurements using singular value decomposition.

The correlation between aortic diameter and stiffness was approximately 0.21, indicating a modest correlation between the two phenotypes. 1 st principal component (PC1) was interpreted as a shared-direction component of diameter and stiffness while 2 nd principal component (PC2) represents their divergent component.
To ensure interpretability, the loading vectors were signed relative to the increasing values of aortic diameter.

Proteome-wide associations using sequential covariate-adjusted models were repeated for PC1 and PC2 as secondary analyses using the same multivariable framework as aortic diameter associations, adjusting for age, sex, ethnicity, BMI, SBP, and smoking status in the fully adjusted model.
PC2 results were considered exploratory.

To gain biological insight into the functions of the proteins driving TAA phenotypes, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) and Over-Representation Analysis (ORA) were performed using the "clusterProfiler" R package (30).

text.text: For GSEA, proteins were ranked continuously by a composite score, which was defined as: Rank = β / SE, where β is the multivariable regression coefficient from the primary fully adjusted model (Model 5 for aortic diameter and Model 6 for stiffness) and SE is the standard error.
The ranked list was subsequently enriched according to the MSigDB Hallmark (H), Curated Gene Sets (C2), and Biological Processes (C5) human gene set collections using 10,000 permutations.
Multiple-testing correction was applied separately within each phenotype and gene-set collection using the Benjamini-Hochberg method.
This analysis was performed separately for each imaging phenotype.
The ORA was applied to evaluate discrete, threshold-based protein lists derived from phenotypic interactions.
This included proteins significantly associated across both the diameter and PC1 phenotypes and proteins uniquely associated with individual phenotypes.
These proteins were enriched according to Gene Ontology: Biological Processes (GO:BP) via the "org.Hs.eg.db" human annotations database (31).
text.formatted: These proteins were enriched according to Gene Ontology: Biological Processes (GO:BP) via the "org.Hs.eg.db" human annotations database <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(31)</ref>.

text.text: The ORA used successfully mapped Olink-tested proteins as the background universe.
Enriched pathways with an FDR-adjusted p-value < 0.05 were selected.
text.formatted: Enriched pathways with an FDR-adjusted p-value < 0.05 were selected.

text.text: Protein-protein interaction analysis was performed as an exploratory follow-up for protein subsets showing significant ORA enrichment after FDR adjustment.
This approach was used to visualize the relationships among enriched proteins.

Given the significant role of extracellular matrix degradation in thoracic aortic aneurysm and the well-documented link between elastin (ELN) and thoracic aortic disease (4,5,32), a sensitivity analysis was conducted centred around the ELN levels in the cohort.

Associations between circulating ELN and each aortic phenotype were sequentially fitted across three ordinary least squares (OLS) models for both the individual metrics (stiffness and diameter) and the combined phenotype based on PC1: 1) unadjusted model based on the raw, unadjusted association between ELN and phenotype; 2) age-adjusted model; 3) fully adjusted model, controlled for the full baseline variables.
Additionally, to determine whether proteomic associations with thoracic aortic phenotypes vary by biological sex, the associations were tested via sex-interaction testing.
For each protein, an ANOVA-based likelihood ratio test (LRT) was used to compare between the main-effects model and an interactions model including the term Sex × Phenotype.
Interaction p-values were adjusted according to the BH method.

Sexstratified multivariable linear regressions were executed separately within female and male subgroups, adjusting for age, ethnicity, BMI, SBP and smoking status in the diameter phenotype models and excluding SBP for the stiffness phenotype models.
Subgroup p-values were independently FDR-adjusted using the BH method.
The final cohort, restricted to participants with both proteomic and imaging data available yielded a study sample of n = 6,773.

text.text: Among the associated proteins with aortic diameter, tetraspanin-1 (TSPAN1), follitropin subunit beta (FSHB), glycodelin (PAEP), chordin-like protein 2 (CHRDL2), and leptin (LEP) were the most significantly influenced by sex interactions.

FSHB, PAEP, TSPAN1, glycoprotein hormones alpha chain (CGA), and receptor-type tyrosine-protein phosphatase zeta (PTPRZ1) were among those associated with aortic stiffness that were significantly influenced by sex interactions.
In this cross-sectional proteome-wide association study, aortic diameter and stiffness showed markedly different circulating proteomic profiles.
In the baseline ageand sex-adjusted analyses, 358 proteins were associated with diameter and 60 with aortic stiffness following FDR correction.
Subsequent additions of covariate adjustments indicated that these associations were sensitive to cardiometabolic covariates, particularly BMI.

Across the fully adjusted multivariable linear regression models, aortic diameter was associated with a broad proteomic signature (417 proteins), whereas stiffness was associated with a more restricted proteomic signature (6 proteins).

Functional enrichment analyses further revealed differences between the two imaging phenotypes: thoracic aortic diameter was characterized predominantly by complement/coagulation pathways, while stiffness showed a more distinct profile involving cytokinesis, cytoskeletal organization and intracellular transport.

Secondary PCA-derived analysis showed that PC1, representing the same-direction component between aortic diameter and stiffness, largely overlapped with the diameter-associated proteomic profile, with 310 out of the 370 proteins being shared in the fully adjusted models.

These findings extend prior genetic, imaging and proteomic work by linking largescale plasma proteomics to imaging-derived thoracic aortic phenotypes, and by directly comparing the molecular profiles of structural dilation and functional stiffening.
Prior work on the UK Biobank dataset has demonstrated that automated cardiac MRI-derived aortic diameter can be used for genetic analysis and predict future TAA risk (13).
Our study builds on this by examining whether circulating plasma proteins are associated with continuous thoracic aortic imaging phenotypes, rather than focusing solely on the genetic determinants.
Other similar proteomics work conducted in TAA patient populations have been limited to smaller sample sizes and restricted to clinically diagnosed aneurysm events (16, (34) (35) (36) (37).

text.text: The current approach may capture earlier biological variation across different aspects of aortic remodelling before patients meet clinical thresholds for a diagnosis of TAA.

Current clinical surveillance and intervention decisions remain largely diameter-based, with guideline recommendations using aortic size to classify aneurysmal dilation and determine imaging follow-up (4, 5).

text.text: From a clinical perspective, diameter and stiffness may capture different aspects or stages of thoracic aortic remodelling.
Aortic diameter reflects the structural enlargement of the vasculature and remains the established metric for surveillance and intervention thresholds (4, 5).
text.formatted: Aortic diameter reflects the structural enlargement of the vasculature and remains the established metric for surveillance and intervention thresholds <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">5)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, stiffness reflects the mechanical properties of the aortic wall and may be influenced by vascular ageing, extracellular matrix composition, and vascular smooth muscle cell function (8).
text.formatted: In contrast, stiffness reflects the mechanical properties of the aortic wall and may be influenced by vascular ageing, extracellular matrix composition, and vascular smooth muscle cell function <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(8)</ref>.

text.text: Previous work has suggested that aortic stiffness may act as a potential marker for adverse cardiovascular outcomes and dissection among patients with a dilated ascending aorta (9, 10).
text.formatted: Previous work has suggested that aortic stiffness may act as a potential marker for adverse cardiovascular outcomes and dissection among patients with a dilated ascending aorta <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">10)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, it is possible that aortic diameter and stiffness do not occur synchronously but may instead occur distinctly or temporally separated in the disease progression.

The differing proteomic patterns observed in this study are consistent with these findings in the literature, although the cross-sectional design prevents verification of the temporal sequence of events.
Sequential covariate adjustment also found that the observed proteomic associations were substantially influenced by cardiometabolic factors.

For aortic diameter, adjustment for BMI substantially attenuated the magnitude of several leading protein associations, whereas additional adjustment for SBP generally produced smaller changes once BMI was accounted for.
Further inclusion of both smoking status and ethnicity resulted in comparatively modest additional changes, suggesting that much of the covariate-related variation was accounted for by BMI and SBP.
Similarly, substantial attenuation was associated with additional adjustment of BMI in the stiffness phenotype model, with only six of 60 proteins remaining significant.
However, incorporating SBP in the sensitivity analyses substantially increased the number of significant proteinphenotype associations.
Given the direct inclusion of SBP in the derivation of the stiffness phenotype, the primary stiffness model excluded SBP from adjustment.

It is also important to note that the observed impact of the covariates may not necessarily be evidence of confounding alone; BMI and blood pressure may also act as mediators linking circulating proteins to aortic remodelling, which this cross-sectional design cannot distinguish.
A key finding was the biological difference underlying aortic diameter and stiffness changes.

Aortic diameter was associated with hundreds of proteins in the fully adjusted model, with most showing inverse associations (388/417 proteins), whereas stiffness had a much more restricted molecular signature (six proteins) in the primary fully adjusted model.
This suggests that aortic diameter and stiffness should not be treated as interchangeable measures of the same disease process.

The broader diameter-associated signature seems to reflect more extensive changes affecting various types of proteins, while stiffness may capture a more restricted phenotype reflecting weaker effect sizes, greater variability between patients, differences in biological processes between diameter and stiffness, or any combination of these factors.

The secondary PCA analysis found mostly similar diameter-associated signals; however, 55 proteins were uniquely associated with PC1, suggesting that combining the two aortic phenotypes may capture additional proteomic signal not detected by either alone.
Complement and coagulation pathways represented one of the most consistent signals associated with aortic diameter.

Negative enrichment was observed across Hallmark, C2 curated pathways and GO Biological Processes collections, indicating that these proteins tended to show inverse associations with increasing diameter.

Although complement and coagulation pathways have previously been implicated as activated processes in aneurysmal biology, contributing to aortic medial degeneration through regulation of matrix metalloproteinases, the functional enrichment analysis from this present study identified negative enrichment with increasing aortic diameter (38, 39).

text.text: This may reflect potential differences between systemic levels of proteins and local aortic wall activity.

Complement factors, such as C3b, have been shown to deposit within the aortic wall (40), alongside increased expression of complement receptors (38), potentially contributing to local consumption of the proteins.

text.text: A proteomic analysis of TAA at both tissue and plasma levels has also identified complement and coagulation cascades across both scales, supporting their involvement.

Additionally, this may reflect important methodological distinctions, with previous studies primarily having examined complement activation within aneurysmal tissue models or patients with established thoracic aortic disease (38) (39) (40), whereas the present analysis evaluated circulating plasma proteins across a wide continuum of imaging phenotypes.

text.text: Diameter was additionally enriched for extracellular-matrix and contractile pathways, including matrisome, ECM regulators, and sarcomere organization.

These findings are biologically consistent with the pathophysiology of TAA, characterized by medial degeneration, extracellular-matrix disruption, and vascular smooth muscle dysfunction (41) (42) (43) (44).

text.text: Other proteomics analyses have also previously shown similar findings (34).

text.text: In contrast, although only 6 proteins were associated with stiffness after FDR correction and covariate adjustment, GSEA of the ranked proteome showed a more distinct enrichment profile.

GO Biological Process analysis highlighted cell-cycle, mitotic, cytokinesis, cytoskeletal organisation and intracellular transport pathways, while the C2 collection enrichment suggested cytokine signalling, glycosaminoglycan synthesis and EGFR signalling.
This is consistent with functional enrichment analyses of proteins identified in patients with aortic aneurysm (45, 46).
text.formatted: This is consistent with functional enrichment analyses of proteins identified in patients with aortic aneurysm <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(45,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">46)</ref>.

text.text: However, considering only six proteins reached FDR significance for stiffness, the findings from stiffness may reflect weaker protein-level effects, and require validated in other independent cohorts.
The limited overlap across the two phenotype models is biologically informative and may help prioritize candidate circulating biomarkers for future biomarker investigation.
REN, BCAN, GGH and THY1 were the only proteins significantly associated with diameter, stiffness and the secondary PC1 phenotype in the fully adjusted models.
Notably, REN is known to be important in the renin-angiotensinaldosterone system (RAAS) in blood pressure regulation and vascular remodelling (47).
text.formatted: Notably, REN is known to be important in the renin-angiotensinaldosterone system (RAAS) in blood pressure regulation and vascular remodelling <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(47)</ref>.

text.text: BCAN is a type of proteoglycan, belonging to the lectican family, members of which have been implicated in proteoglycan accumulation and medial degeneration in TAA (48).
text.formatted: BCAN is a type of proteoglycan, belonging to the lectican family, members of which have been implicated in proteoglycan accumulation and medial degeneration in TAA <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(48)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, THY1 may reflect immune or cell adhesion pathways when responding to paracrine signals to promote proliferation and vasculogenesis (49, 50).
text.formatted: Additionally, THY1 may reflect immune or cell adhesion pathways when responding to paracrine signals to promote proliferation and vasculogenesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(49,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">50)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the small number of overlapping proteins suggests that thoracic aortic remodelling involves partly overlapping but mostly phenotype-specific molecular processes.

The observed protein-phenotype associations may have several explanations, including a causal effect of circulating proteins on aortic remodelling, residual or shared confounding, or reverse causation whereby changes in aortic function influence circulating protein levels.
Given the cross-sectional nature of this study, these possibilities cannot be distinguished.

From a translational perspective, an important future direction will be to determine whether the circulating proteomic signatures identified in this study can provide incremental predictive value beyond the established imaging-derived aortic diameter and risk factors (13, 51).
text.formatted: From a translational perspective, an important future direction will be to determine whether the circulating proteomic signatures identified in this study can provide incremental predictive value beyond the established imaging-derived aortic diameter and risk factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">51)</ref>.

text.text: Multimodal risk models combining established variables with selected circulating proteins should be evaluated longitudinally for their ability to predict incident TAA.

Such models may also help determine at what stage proteomic changes associated with aortic stiffness occurs relative to those accompanying structural dilation, thereby clarifying whether these phenotypes capture different stages of disease progression.

Conversely, establishing individual proteins as causal mediators or therapeutic targets would require complementary genetic approaches, such as Mendelian randomisation, experimental validation, and ultimately interventional clinical studies.
Exploratory sex-interaction analyses additionally suggested that some proteinphenotype associations may differ between male and female participants.

Notably, among these proteins, LEP demonstrated a stronger inverse relationship with aortic diameter and stiffness in females than males, and BCAN demonstrated a greater magnitude of effect on aortic stiffness in men.

However, these analyses were exploratory, and future studies should investigate how sex modifies proteomic signatures of aortic remodelling, particularly given the known impact of sex on thoracic aortic aneurysm progression and outcomes (52) (53) (54).

text.text: One limitation of this present study is its cross-sectional design, which limits inference about temporality or causality.
Further Mendelian randomisation analyses based on an external GWAS dataset or other causal-inference approaches may help assess whether these proteins have a causal role.
Related to this, plasma proteomic samples and cardiac imaging were collected at different UK Biobank visits.

Although one analysis integrating UK Biobank proteomics with multi-organ imaging found that this temporal gap did not have a significant impact on the associations (22), the possibility that circulating protein levels changed between the visits could not nevertheless be excluded.

text.text: The sequential covariate analyses cannot determine whether changes in protein-phenotype associations following adjustment for BMI and SBP reflect minimizing confounding effects or adjustment for factors lying on the causal pathway.
Second, the level of circulating proteins may not necessarily reflect aortic tissue-specific changes and may reflect other systemic changes.
Third, the UK Biobank contains mostly volunteers who are predominantly white (96.07%) and healthier than the general population, limiting generalizability (55).
text.formatted: Third, the UK Biobank contains mostly volunteers who are predominantly white (96.07%) and healthier than the general population, limiting generalizability <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(55)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, Olink proteomics measures a predefined panel of proteins rather than the complete list of circulating proteins.
Fifth, this study did not adjust for kidney function (eGFR).

Renin, in particular, is influenced by kidney function and other determinants of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (56); it is possible that the observed association is partially reflected by these residual confounders rather than aortic biology.
text.formatted: Renin, in particular, is influenced by kidney function and other determinants of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(56)</ref>; it is possible that the observed association is partially reflected by these residual confounders rather than aortic biology.

text.text: Circulating proteomic associations with thoracic aortic remodelling differed considerably between structural dilation and functional stiffening and were influenced by adjustment for cardiometabolic factors.

Aortic diameter was characterized by complement-coagulation, extracellular matrix, and contractile signatures, whereas stiffness showed a smaller but more distinct pattern involving cytokine and proliferative signalling, cell cycle regulation, and intracellular transport.
Secondary PCA analysis suggested that the same-direction component between diameter and stiffness largely reflected the diameter-associated proteomic profile.
These findings suggest partly overlapping but differing proteomic association patterns underlying thoracic aortic remodelling across structural dilation and functional stiffening.
Proteins associated with both aortic dilation and stiffness may provide a starting point for biomarker discovery, although longitudinal and external validation are further required.
